prompt:
Dockview layout serialization, versioning and restore. Question: For dockview-vue (Dockview 8.6 [TARGET]) in a Vue 3.5
[TARGET] app, what is the exact API for serializing the full layout
(groups, panels, tabs, sizes, floating windows, popout windows) to
JSON and restoring it on startup, and what is the recommended
practice for versioning that JSON so old saved layouts migrate
cleanly when panel types change? Cover what `toJSON`/`fromJSON`
capture and what they omit (e.g. per-panel view state), and how to
handle a saved layout that references a panel type the new version
no longer ships.

Wanted answer format: a short version-compatibility table (Dockview
version rows, serialize/restore API columns), then minimal Vue code
sketches for save, restore and migration, then a bullet list of
things `toJSON` omits, each with its source link.

Why it matters: Dockview owns presentation state only
(positions, sizes, tabs, popouts), serialised per user profile, and
is never authority. The architect must design the profile store and
the migration path before any panel ships.

Restoring large Dockview layouts without jank. Question: In a Dockview-based IDE-style shell (dockview-vue) with
many panels (surface wall, fleet, inspector, timeline, terminal
drawer), what are the documented or community-proven techniques to
restore a saved layout at startup without visible popping, layout
thrash, or progressive flashing? Cover deferred panel
creation, placeholder panels, suspending layout events during
restore, and measured guidance on how many panels restore
acceptably on typical desktop hardware.

Wanted answer format: ranked list of techniques (most effective
first), each with a short explanation, a minimal code
sketch, and a source link; close with open pitfalls (what still
flashes and why).

Why it matters: the product is an F11 [TARGET] full-screen wall that
must boot to a settled multi-panel layout; startup jank breaks the
monitoring-desk experience and destabilizes visual test baselines.

Dockview popout windows in Electron: one window per popout. Question: When Dockview pops a panel out inside Electron, what is the
recommended architecture: does each popout become a separate
Electron BrowserWindow, and how do the main window and popout
windows share state, synchronize the layout model, route IPC, and
handle the popout window closing (docking the panel back vs
destroying it)? Cover the dockview-vue popout API surface, what the
library does versus what the host app must implement, and known
limitations (events that do not cross windows, drag-back behavior).

Wanted answer format: an architecture diagram in words (numbered
components and numbered message flows), followed by a table of
responsibilities (Dockview-owned vs app-owned rows), followed by a
limitations list with source links.

Why it matters: every UI layer is a capsule panel able to pop out
[TARGET], and F11 [TARGET] kiosk uses a dedicated BrowserWindow while
popouts become extra BrowserWindows for multi-monitor walls. The
architect must own the cross-window protocol.

Multi-monitor Electron walls, including Wayland. Question: What is the current state of running an Electron app
across several monitors as a video wall (a dedicated full-screen window per
display, windows following displays on hot-plug, per-display DPI),
and what specifically breaks or differs under Linux Wayland versus
X11 (window positioning APIs, full-screen/kiosk behavior, display
enumeration, drag between windows)? Include the relevant Electron
APIs (`screen` module, `BrowserWindow` placement options) and any
documented Wayland gaps.

Wanted answer format: a platform matrix (Windows, macOS, X11,
Wayland columns; placement, fullscreen, DPI, hot-plug rows) with
support status per cell, then a Wayland-specific gaps list with
source links, then recommended fallback behavior per gap.

Why it matters: security-monitoring desks are multi-monitor walls,
and whether Dockview popouts fit multi-monitor walls under Wayland
is an explicit AUSENTE open question in the architecture inputs.

OpenVue theming API: tokens, presets, dark mode. Question: OpenVue is the MIT-licensed continuation of PrimeVue
(PrimeVue 5 [TARGET] is no longer MIT). What is its theming
architecture: how are design tokens defined (CSS custom properties,
preset objects, or both), how does an app override primitive,
semantic and component-level tokens, how do light/dark/high-contrast
modes switch at runtime, and how stable is this API across recent
OpenVue releases? Include how scoped versus global theming works in
a Vue 3.5 [TARGET] + Vite app.

Wanted answer format: a layered diagram in words (primitive,
semantic, component token layers with override points), minimal
override code sketches (global preset plus a component-level
override plus runtime dark-mode switch), and a stability note per
API with source links.

Why it matters: the app must map the OpenVue theme and the Dockview
theme onto the same tokens so the app reads as visually unified. The
architect needs the exact override points before writing any
component CSS.

OpenVue maturity, cadence and fallback planning. Question: What is the public maturity signal for OpenVue (the PrimeVue
continuation) as a dependency for a commercial app: release cadence,
maintainer responsiveness, issue/backlog trend, Vue version support
policy, breaking-change history, and adoption size? And what is the
practical cost of the documented fallback (PrimeVue v4 [TARGET]):
which OpenVue component APIs differ from PrimeVue v4 so that a
fallback would require adapter work?

Wanted answer format: a maturity scorecard table (dimension rows,
finding plus evidence-link columns), then a fallback-cost section
listing API differences by component family with estimated adapter
size (small/medium/large) per family.

Why it matters: OpenVue is young with thin public signals, and the
inputs mandate pinning it exactly while keeping a fallback. The
architect must quantify that risk and pre-design the adapter seam.

One token system feeding two libraries. Question: What are the proven patterns for running a unified
CSS-custom-property token system (primitive/semantic/component
layers, light/dark/high-contrast themes, density variants) underneath
third-party libraries with their own theming systems — here
OpenVue components and Dockview layout chrome — in a Vue 3 app?
Cover token naming and layering conventions (e.g. Style Dictionary,
Token Studio / W3C format), build-time export of a static CSS file,
runtime theme switching without a flash, and how to handle tokens
a library requires but the shared system does not define.

Wanted answer format: a recommended layering diagram in words, a
naming-convention table with examples, a build/runtime pipeline
description (tools plus file flow), and an edge-case list (missing
tokens, unit conflicts, density interplay) with a resolution per
case, all with source links.

Why it matters: versioned primitive/semantic/component tokens with
complete allowed overrides and deterministic offline CSS export are
gated requirements (C-TOKEN), and a silent contradictory theme is an
explicit must-fail case. The token pipeline is load-bearing.

PTY broker patterns: backpressure, multiplexing, reload survival. Question: For a VS Code-style bottom terminal drawer built on
@xterm/xterm 6 [TARGET] in the renderer and node-pty in a utility
process (a dedicated PTY per session), what are the recommended patterns
for: framing messages between renderer and broker (session id,
sequence numbers), backpressure when the renderer lags (pausing the
PTY), separating input and output channels, reattaching sessions
after a renderer reload, and bounding scrollback memory per tab?
Include how popular Electron apps structure the broker (utility
process vs main) and its supervision.

Wanted answer format: a message-flow description with a frame
schema example, then a pattern per concern (backpressure,
reattach, scrollback cap, supervision) with a minimal code sketch
and source link each, then an anti-pattern list.

Why it matters: the drawer hosts AI sessions that launch prompts
toward capsules, with typed {session, seq, bytes} frames and a
session list that must survive renderer reload. The broker protocol
is part of the security boundary.

node-pty and terminal-input security in a sandboxed renderer. Question: What are the known security considerations for embedding
node-pty plus xterm.js in an Electron app with a sandboxed renderer
(`sandbox:true`, `contextIsolation:true`,
`nodeIntegration:false`): PTY escape-sequence attacks against the
terminal emulator, malicious output that tricks copy/paste or
clickable links, environment inheritance by the spawned shell,
working-directory and binary-path pinning, and safe handling of
pasted or bracketed content? Include xterm.js parser hardening
options and Electron-side mitigations (utility-process isolation,
allowlisted spawn config).

Wanted answer format: a threat table (threat, affected layer,
mitigation, residual risk columns) with source links, then a
hardened spawn-configuration checklist, then xterm.js settings to
enable or avoid.

Why it matters: the drawer must never auto-execute arriving text
and must keep secrets out of UI and logs, while AI sessions will
routinely display untrusted model output inside the terminal. The
threat model must be explicit before the drawer ships.

Stable ids, roles and names as an agent contract. Question: What are the established patterns for exposing a stable,
machine-operable element contract from a complex web UI: stable
element ids that survive re-renders and virtualization, ARIA roles
and accessible names as the addressing vocabulary, and element
geometry in window CSS pixels — such that an external agent can
observe (snapshot the tree) and act (target an element) reliably?
Cover id-generation schemes (semantic vs hashed), how virtualized
lists keep row identity across scroll/sort/filter, and how
 frameworks (Vue, React) preserve or break id stability.

Wanted answer format: a contract checklist (id/role/name/box rules,
a line each with rationale), then per-concern guidance
(virtualization, shadow DOM, modals, focus) with source links, then
common breakages with fixes.

Why it matters: the whole program must be AI-operable through
stable element ids, roles, accessible names and window-pixel boxes
[TARGET], and application IDs must stay distinct from
DOM/CDP/fingerprint handles. This contract is the agent lane's UI
half.

Consuming the accessibility tree: CDP, AT-SPI and in-app export. Question: Compare the practical ways an agent harness obtains
a UI element tree with boxes from an Electron/Chromium app: (a) the
Chrome DevTools Protocol Accessibility domain, (b) OS accessibility
APIs such as Linux AT-SPI (including the
`force-renderer-accessibility` switch), and (c) an in-app semantic
export built by the app itself. Compare fidelity (names, roles,
boxes, states), performance overhead, taint and security side
effects (does attaching CDP/DevTools change app behavior or
security posture?), and suitability for retail versus test-only
builds.

Wanted answer format: a comparison table (fidelity, overhead,
taint/security, retail-suitability rows; per-approach columns)
with source links, then a recommendation per build type (retail,
test, fixture) with reasons.

Why it matters: retail automation/observation must be inert (no
AX-domain enable, no automation walks, no capturePage), while test
mode uses AT-SPI because CDP would taint the launcher. The choice
of observation channel is a security decision, not just tooling.

Live-surface transport: canvas, WebGL, WebRTC, shared memory. Question: For an Electron wall showing many simultaneous live
surfaces (remote Linux framebuffers arriving as raw RGB frames),
compare the transport-and-draw options into the renderer: MJPEG or
H.264 over a local socket into `<canvas>`/`<video>`, WebRTC video
tracks, shared-memory frames via an Electron-side bridge, and
direct WebGL texture upload. Compare per-surface CPU, memory,
latency, implementation complexity, and how each scales with surface
count, citing measured numbers where published.

Wanted answer format: a comparison table (CPU, memory, latency,
complexity, scaling rows; option columns) with numbers plus source
links, then a decision guide (choose X when …), then open
measurement questions for our own benchmarks.

Why it matters: frame transport into the renderer is an explicit
AUSENTE item needing measurement against latency and RSS budgets,
with a reference of 4 capsules at 26–31 fps [CITED: docs/HOLDINGS_LESSONS_UI_ORCHESTRATOR.md:84-84].
The architect must pick the transport before the Surface panel
exists.

Frame pacing, hidden-panel discipline and renderer budgets. Question: What are the best practices for sustaining many live
canvas/WebGL surfaces in a shared Chromium renderer without dropping
the UI frame budget: per-surface draw scheduling (rAF fan-out vs
offscreen canvas vs worker-driven presentation), stopping draws
for folded/hidden panels while keeping capture alive upstream,
bounding GPU and RSS growth, and detecting main-thread long
tasks attributable to surface drawing? Include Electron/Chromium
flags and APIs that help (background throttling behavior,
visibility signals, frame-rate caps).

Wanted answer format: a practice per concern (scheduling, hidden
discipline, memory bounds, long-task attribution), each with a
mechanism description, a minimal code or config sketch, and a
source link; close with a measurement checklist for a wall
benchmark.

Why it matters: frames must stay out of Vue reactivity, folded
panels must stop drawing while capture continues, and input
budgets (authored JS chunk, input-to-present p95 [TARGET]) are
gated. Draw scheduling is where those budgets are won or lost.

Pinia versus plain stores for a snapshot-driven renderer. Question: For a Vue 3.5 [TARGET] renderer that is strictly
non-authoritative — it renders immutable core snapshots
(versioned by schema/epoch/revision/query) and submits intents,
never mutating domain state — compare Pinia stores versus plain
reactive stores (or composable-held state) on: boilerplate for
snapshot replacement, devtools and test ergonomics, SSR-style
hydration analogies, subscription lifecycle (install before
request, dispose on navigation/epoch change), and protection
against accidental local domain mutation. Is there a documented
pattern for marking stores read-only to view code?

Wanted answer format: a comparison table (criterion rows; Pinia,
plain-store, hybrid columns) with a verdict per row,
then a recommended store layout (named stores and their contents)
for this snapshot/intent split, with source links.

Why it matters: the renderer must separate the last admitted
public projection from route, focus, selection and component-local
state, with pure transitions and no writable UI copy becoming
authority. The store shape enforces that law.

Keeping heavy objects out of Vue reactivity. Question: What are the exact Vue 3 reactivity escape hatches and
their pitfalls for an app that moves heavy non-UI objects (video
frames, terminal buffers, large tables) through components:
`shallowRef`, `shallowReactive`, `markRaw`, `triggerRef`, raw
extracts — which operations still traverse or proxy, what breaks
with devtools or HMR, and what are the recommended component
patterns (props down as raw, events up, explicit invalidation) so
templates never deeply observe a frame buffer? Include Vitest
patterns for asserting non-reactivity.

Wanted answer format: an API table (hatch, what it exempts, what
still reacts, gotcha columns) with source links, then
component-pattern sketches (surface panel, terminal tab), then a
test-pattern sketch asserting a frame object stays raw.

Why it matters: frames must never enter Vue reactivity, and
virtualized tables carry tight node budgets (row, overscan and
cell caps [TARGET]). An accidental deep-reactive frame buffer
breaks both budgets at once.

Sandboxed-renderer baseline: flags, CSP, fuses, policy. Question: What is the current recommended Electron security
baseline for a new desktop app shipping a sandboxed renderer:
renderer flags (`sandbox`, `contextIsolation`, `nodeIntegration`,
`nodeIntegrationInWorker`, `webSecurity`, `webviewTag`,
`allowRunningInsecureContent`), Content-Security-Policy starter
for bundled `app://`-style schemes, Electron fuses to set at
package time, permission/navigation/window-open policies, and
macOS entitlement and signing notes (Chromium sandbox vs Apple
App Sandbox)? Note anything that changed in recent Electron
major versions.

Wanted answer format: a baseline checklist grouped by layer
(flags, CSP, fuses, policy, platform), each item with recommended
value, a brief rationale and a source link, then a
recent-changes section (what moved in the last few majors).

Why it matters: the shell security laws fix each of these
values (sandboxed renderer, restrictive CSP, package-time fuses,
default-deny permissions) under release-blocking gates. Research
confirms the baseline is current before the template is cut.

Preload and IPC hardening: facades, guards, schema validation. Question: What are the current best practices for hardening the
Electron preload/IPC boundary: exposing a minimal contextBridge
facade of domain operations instead of transport primitives,
validating the sender frame/origin on every IPC message in main,
allowlisting channels and operations, schema-validating payloads
(including byte/integer bounds and closed enums), versioning the
facade, and testing the boundary (negative tests with forged
senders and oversized payloads)? Include utility-process message
ports (MessageChannelMain) guidance.

Wanted answer format: a practice-per-layer guide (preload shape,
main guard, schema validation, versioning, tests), each with a
minimal code sketch and source link, then a negative-test
checklist (forged sender, wrong origin, oversized payload, stale
epoch, unknown operation).

Why it matters: renderer-supplied identity is data, every
privileged receiver must validate sender/ownership/schema/bounds/
epoch/slot before effects, and stale replies must die on service
restart. The preload facade is the most-attacked seam.

Playwright for Electron versus a test-owned main. Question: Compare Electron end-to-end strategies: (a)
Playwright's Electron driver (launch, window handles, CDP-backed
selectors and screenshots) versus (b) a test-owned main process
that drives input via `webContents.sendInputEvent` and reads state
through app-owned seams. Compare selector and assertion power,
pixel-capture support, determinism (fixed geometry, font
pinning), process-teardown strictness, CI cost and flakiness, and
— critically — whether each approach perturbs the app under test
(CDP/DevTools taint, automation latches, timing distortion).
Include how each handles multi-window (popout) apps.

Wanted answer format: a comparison table (criterion rows;
Playwright, test-owned-main columns) with source links, then
a verdict per test layer (component, journey, battery, visual)
naming which strategy fits and why, then migration notes (what a
Playwright suite keeps if the project switches).

Why it matters: CDP/DevTools automation taints the Holdings
launcher, so the proven route is a test-owned main — but
Playwright must be evaluated against that lesson before adoption.
This question is that evaluation.

Shipping an Electron game on Steam: depots, DLC, overlay, Cloud. Question: What is the current practical guide to shipping an
Electron game on Steam: SteamPipe depot layout for Electron apps
(shared runtime vs per-OS depots, native modules outside ASAR),
Steamworks SDK integration options from Node/Electron
(`steamworks.js` vs `steamworks-rs` vs minimal bindings), DLC
ownership and installation checks at runtime (which SDK calls
prove what, and their documented non-guarantees), Game Overlay
compatibility with Chromium/Electron renderers, Steam Cloud save
rules for opaque slot files, and achievements/stats pump threading
(independent of rAF and pause)? Include signing/notarization notes
per OS.

Wanted answer format: a section per concern (depots, SDK choice,
DLC checks, overlay, Cloud, achievements, signing), each with
recommended practice, a gotcha list and source links; the DLC
section must include a call-vs-meaning table (SDK call,
what it proves, what it must never be taken to prove).

Why it matters: SteamPipe is the sole updater, DLC checks have a
formal signal/meaning/forbidden-inference contract, persisted DLC
state is only a UI cache, and callbacks must never grant economic
effects. The Steam adapter design depends on these ground truths.

AI disclosure obligations for Steam games with in-game agents. Question: What disclosure obligations apply to a Steam game whose
core loop includes AI agents (in-game rival firms driven by
bundled models, plus an AI assistant that operates the game UI):
Steam store-page AI-content disclosure rules (what must be
declared, where, and how enforcement works), any platform or
regional overlay (consumer-protection or AI-transparency rules
affecting games), how comparable shipped games phrase their
disclosures (examples with links), and what changes if models run
locally/bundled versus remotely hosted? Exclude speculation; cite
current store rules and rules-in-force only.

Wanted answer format: an obligations table (obligation, source
rule, where it surfaces in the product/store page, evidence link),
then quoted real-world disclosure examples with
links, then a local-vs-remote differences section, then an
explicit list of what remains interpretation rather than rule.

Why it matters: Holdings ships on Steam as an AI-assisted
management game [TARGET] with bundled Python agents as T2 clients
and AI operation of the UI itself. Disclosure text and placement
must be designed into the store page and the game, not retrofitted.

Orchestrator chat drawer UX. In 2025-2026 desktop apps built with Electron and Vue (or similar), what are the best UX and implementation patterns for a bottom drop-up chat/terminal drawer, like the customer-support chat widgets on websites, that acts as an orchestrator: one composer sends a prompt to one, several or all AI agent sessions (each in its own terminal panel), shows per-session status (idle, busy, done, error) and streams results back? Cover targeting UI, mentions and selection, broadcast confirmation, keyboard shortcuts, collapsed and expanded states, accessibility, and known open-source examples. Answer as a pattern list with pros and cons and links.

Repository layout for AI code generation and surgical context retrieval. What repository and file-organisation conventions (2025-2026) make a Vue 3 + TypeScript + Electron codebase easiest for AI coding agents to navigate and edit precisely? Cover one concern per file, file size limits, index or barrel files, llms.txt and AGENTS.md conventions, symbol naming, colocated tests, docs per component, and evidence or case studies of their effect on AI agent accuracy. Answer as concrete rules with sources.

Sharing one UI kit across two Electron apps. What is the best way (2025-2026) to share one Vue 3 UI kit (design tokens, themed component wrappers, Dockview panel shells, terminal panel) between two separate Electron apps in different repositories? Compare a git submodule, a private npm package, vendored copies with a sync script, and a monorepo with workspaces, covering versioning, CI, licence notices and AI-agent friendliness. Answer with a recommendation and its trade-offs.
